picks.why: Dernau family estate on the valley's steep slate, a house of the turn to dry, barrel aged Spätburgunder in the 1980s; the Pfarrwingert is its Grosses Gewächs, the Ahr's red in one glass.
picks.note: Confirm the label's form for the years taught (Dernauer Pfarrwingert or Dernau Pfarrwingert) and date the dry turn only from two sources; the Walporzheimer Kräuterberg GG goes in others. Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Rech family estate of the middle valley; the Herrenberg, a steep slope of slate above the village and a VDP Grosse Lage, gives its Spätburgunder Grosses Gewächs.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. The sources disagree on the house's age (winemaking from 1578 in one, a winery since 1900 in another): leave founded empty unless two agree. Confirm the soil of the site and the oak regime from the house; name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Ahrweiler family estate that holds the whole of the Gärkammer at Walporzheim, which the VDP calls the smallest of its Grosse Lagen in Germany, planted to Spätburgunder alone and named, the VDP says, for the heat it holds in summer.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. The VDP's own pages are the primary for the monopole, its size among the Grosse Lagen and the name; confirm the label's form (Walporzheimer or Walporzheim Gärkammer) and name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Mayschoss estate of the upper valley, a VDP house making Spätburgunder and Frühburgunder; the Mönchberg above the village, a Grosse Lage, gives its Grosses Gewächs.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Decanter dates the estate's records to 1574 and a wine encyclopedia calls it the Mönchberg's largest holder: give either only with a second source. Confirm the label's form; name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Dernau family estate known for Spätburgunder and Frühburgunder; its Grosses Gewächs of Spätburgunder comes from the Hardtberg at Dernau, so the group shows Dernau's second Grosse Lage beside Meyer-Näkel's Pfarrwingert.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Decanter names the Hardtberg GG as the house's own and dates the estate to 1953: confirm both in a second source and the label's form. The Mayschoss cooperative of 1868, the oldest in Germany by the region record, is the valley's history and may be told in a story, not a pick.

picks.why: Oberhausen family estate of 1750 by the library's date, which carried the Nahe onto lists abroad; the Hermannshöhle at Niederhausen gives its dry Grosses Gewächs, and the library teaches the site as a wine of its own.
picks.note: The library also holds the site as w-hermannshohle: tie the record to p-donnhoff. Confirm 1750 in two sources, the site's soils before naming them, and the label's form; the sweet Oberhäuser Brücke Spätlese from the house's monopole goes in others.

picks.why: Monzingen family estate of the upper Nahe; the Halenberg, a steep slope of blue slate and quartzite by the library's account, gives its Grosses Gewächs, with the Frühlingsplätzchen beside it.
picks.note: Confirm the Halenberg's soils in two sources and the label's form for the years taught; the Halenberg Auslese goes in others. Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Bockenau family estate in a side valley of the Nahe, fermenting with wild yeasts into a smoky, struck match style; the Felseneck above the village gives its Grosses Gewächs.
picks.note: Confirm the Felseneck's soil before naming it and the label's form; the house also holds Kupfergrube and Felsenberg, so say which goes in others. Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Niederhausen estate founded by the Prussian state in 1902 as its Nahe domain, on steep rocky ground that took in an abandoned copper mine; the Kupfergrube, planted on the mine, gives its Grosses Gewächs.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. The Wines of Germany page is the national body's account of the domain: confirm 1902 and the mine's working until 1901 in a second source, tell the sale of 2009 as history with no living name, and confirm whether the house still holds the GG back for a later release.

picks.why: Burg Layen family estate of the lower Nahe, known for Riesling from Dorsheim's Goldloch, Pittermännchen and Burgberg and for its traditional method Sekt; the Goldloch is its Grosses Gewächs to know.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS and not searched in this run: confirm in two sources that the Goldloch GG leads the house's range rather than the Pittermännchen or the Burgberg, the label's form, and the Sekt for others. Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Flörsheim-Dalsheim family estate of the Wonnegau, of 1789 by the library's date, whose dry Rieslings from limestone changed what Rheinhessen meant; G-Max is its dry Riesling from old vines with no site on the label, a wine the library holds on its own.
picks.note: The library also holds the wine as w-g-max: tie the record to p-keller. Confirm in two sources what the house says of G-Max (its first vintage, the parcels, the story of its name) and teach it with nothing that dates. Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Westhofen family estate farmed organically and then biodynamically; the Morstein, limestone of the Wonnegau, gives its Grosses Gewächs, the same site as Keller's read in a rounder house style.
picks.note: Confirm the label's form (Westhofener or Westhofen Morstein) and the date of the biodynamic turn in two sources; Kirchspiel, Brunnenhäuschen and Aulerde go in others. Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Nackenheim estate of 1890 by the library's date, on the Roter Hang; the Rothenberg, the red slate cliff above the Rhine, gives its dry Grosses Gewächs and sweet wines up to Trockenbeerenauslese.
picks.note: Confirm 1890 in two sources and the label's form; the Rothenberg Trockenbeerenauslese goes in others. Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Bodenheim family estate working the red slope's Pettenthal, Hipping, Ölberg and Rothenberg; its Grosses Gewächs from the Pettenthal at Nierstein shows the Roter Hang's smoky, stony Riesling.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. The house's own material puts the Rothenberg wurzelecht, from ungrafted vines, forward as its signature: the Pettenthal is chosen so the page does not show the Rothenberg twice beside Gunderloch, and the author may propose the swap with the checker's agreement. The estate is run with Battenfeld-Spanier by one couple: say so with no names, or leave it out.

picks.why: Hohen-Sülzen family estate in the far south of the Wonnegau, farmed biodynamically on limestone; its Grosses Gewächs from the Frauenberg at Nieder-Flörsheim is the cool, chalky side of the region.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Meininger's tastings put the Frauenberg forward and the house's own material the Zellerweg am Schwarzen Herrgott: confirm in two sources which leads, and the label's form; the Kirchenstück goes in others.

picks.why: Escherndorf family estate above a bend of the Main; its dry Silvaner Grosses Gewächs comes from Am Lumpen 1655, the heart of the steep Lump, and teaches the grape that defines the region.
picks.note: The library writes Escherndorfer Lump Silvaner GG; Falstaff and the house's importer print Am Lumpen 1655: confirm the label's form and that 1655 is the site's first mention, in two sources. Keep the house apart from Weingut Rainer Sauer, a separate Escherndorf estate whose wine from the same site carries the same name. The Lump Trockenbeerenauslese goes in others.

picks.why: Würzburg charitable foundation of 1576 whose vineyards have long paid for its hospital; its Silvaner Grosses Gewächs comes from the Stein, the shell limestone slope above the city that gave Steinwein its name.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS and not searched in this run: confirm 1576 and the founder, Prince Bishop Julius Echter von Mespelbrunn, with his dates, in two sources, and that the Stein rather than the Iphöfer Julius-Echter-Berg is the house's lead Silvaner.

picks.why: Würzburg charitable foundation of 1316, the older of the city's two; the Stein-Harfe, a Grosse Lage within the Stein in its sole ownership, gives its Silvaner Grosses Gewächs, while its Stein-Harfe Rieslings are sweet.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. The house's own pages are the primary for the Stein-Harfe; confirm 1316 and its founder in two sources. The sweet Stein-Harfe Riesling Spätlese goes in others.

picks.why: Bürgstadt family estate of the Mainviereck on red sandstone, the red side of Franken; the Hundsrück is the Grosse Lage of its Spätburgunder, beside the Centgrafenberg.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Confirm in two sources that the Hundsrück rather than the Centgrafenberg is the house's lead Spätburgunder, when it was first bottled alone, and the label's form; the Frühburgunder and the Centgrafenberg go in others. Give the house's namesake dates only from two sources, and name no living member of the family.

picks.why: The princely Castell estate of the Steigerwald, on gypsum Keuper; the Schlossberg below the castle gives its Silvaner Grosses Gewächs, and the house tells of the first Silvaner recorded in Germany, planted at Castell in April 1659.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Confirm the planting of 6 April 1659 in two sources (the house's own page counts for its own claim, hedged), whether the Schlossberg is held alone, and how the house writes its name; tell the princely family's history with no living name.

picks.why: Schwaigern estate of the counts of Neipperg, a family that has championed Lemberger for generations; the Ruthe is the Grosse Lage of its Lemberger Grosses Gewächs, with the Schlossberg beside it.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. The house's own wine list names the Ruthe Lemberger GG; confirm the family's history in two sources and keep its tie to a Saint-Émilion estate as history only, with no living name.

picks.why: Fellbach family estate on the edge of Stuttgart; its Riesling Grosses Gewächs from Gips Marienglas, a parcel of gypsum Keuper at Untertürkheim, shows the white side of a red region.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Falstaff lists both this wine and the Fellbacher Lämmler Lemberger GG the region record names: the Riesling is chosen for the group's spread, and the author may argue for the Lämmler with the checker. Confirm that Marienglas names the gypsum crystal of the soil, and the label's form.

picks.why: Fellbach grower's estate known for Spätburgunder and Lemberger from Keuper; its Spätburgunder Grosses Gewächs comes from the Lämmler, Fellbach's Grosse Lage.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Decanter lists the Lämmler Spätburgunder GG: confirm it in a second source, the founding year only from two, and say the founder, who is living, with no name.

picks.why: Bönnigheim family estate known for barrel aged Lemberger and Spätburgunder; its Lemberger Grosses Gewächs comes from the Michaelsberg.
picks.note: In doubt: a wein.plus list of Lemberger names a Dautel Michaelsberg GG, but this run could not confirm the grape, the village the label prints or that it leads the range. Confirm in two sources, or propose a swap with the checker (Herzog von Württemberg or Wöhrwag).

picks.why: Remstal estate at Stetten east of Stuttgart; its Riesling Grosses Gewächs from the Pulvermächer, a steep slope above the village, shows the Rems valley's white side.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Falstaff lists the Stetten Pulvermächer Riesling GG: confirm it in a second source, the site's soil before naming it, and the house's namesake's dates only from two sources.

picks.why: Malterdingen family estate of the Breisgau, of 1987 by the library's date, whose Burgundian Spätburgunder from limestone made the case for German Pinot Noir; the Bienenberg is the Grosse Lage of its Grosses Gewächs.
picks.note: Confirm 1987 in two sources and the label's form for the years taught (Bienenberg, or its Wildenstein parcel); give the founder his dates only from two sources and his heirs no names. Whether Malterdinger, an old local name for Pinot Noir, may be told needs two sources.

picks.why: Ihringen family estate of the Kaiserstuhl on the volcanic terraces of the Winklerberg; the Häusleboden is the parcel of its Spätburgunder Grosses Gewächs, with Grauburgunder from the same hill.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Falstaff prints the wine as Ihringen Winklerberg Wanne Häusleboden Spätburgunder GG in later years: confirm the label's form for the years taught; the Gras im Ofen Grauburgunder GG goes in others. The founding year and the doctor the house is named for only from two sources.

picks.why: Oberbergen family estate of the Kaiserstuhl, tied to the Schwarzer Adler restaurant and an early voice for dry Baden Pinot in the French manner; its Grauburgunder Grosses Gewächs from the Schlossberg at Achkarren shows the region's white Pinot.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. The VDP's page lists Eichberg and Kirchberg as its Grosse Lagen, and Falstaff the Achkarrer Schlossberg Grauburgunder GG year after year: the Grauburgunder is chosen for the group's spread; confirm it in two sources or swap to the Eichberg Spätburgunder GG with the checker. The house's namesake only with dates from two sources.

picks.why: Neuweier estate by Baden-Baden in the Ortenau whose Mauerberg Riesling goes into the Bocksbeutel, the flask Franken keeps for itself, by a right the estate traces to the castle's lord of 1785.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. The VDP names the Grosse Lage Mauerberg Mauerwein, and labels print both: confirm the form for the years taught. Confirm the planting of 1785 and the Bocksbeutel right in two sources, with Baron Philipp Franz von Knebel-Katzenellenbogen (1733 to 1816), and tell the sale of 2012 as history with no living name.

picks.why: Efringen-Kirchen family estate of the Markgräflerland near Basel, bottling much of its range as Landwein; Jaspis 10hoch4 is its Gutedel, the Markgräflerland's own grape made as a serious white.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Falstaff lists Jaspis 10hoch4 Gutedel, later 10hoch4 Gutedel, and a Jaspis 10hoch4 Spätburgunder: confirm which the house leads with and the label's form; confirm what 10hoch4 means (a planting density is the likely reading) and why the house bottles as Landwein, in two sources. The estate carries its living founder's name in some listings: say the founder. Laible's Achat Riesling of Durbach is the alternative if the checker prefers a second Ortenau house.

picks.why: Bacharach family estate at the Hahnenhof; its Riesling Grosses Gewächs comes from the Hahn, a steep slate slope by the Rhine at Bacharach.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. The VDP lists the Hahn as an Erste Lage while Falstaff prints the GG as Bacharach Im Hahn: confirm the classification and the label's form for the years taught. The house's namesake only with dates from two sources; the family with no names.

picks.why: Steeg family estate in a side valley above Bacharach, known also for traditional method Riesling Sekt; the St. Jost, a VDP Grosse Lage of slate, gives its Grosses Gewächs.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. The VDP's page is the primary for the site and Falstaff lists the GG: confirm the label's form and the Sekt in two sources; the Wolfshöhle goes in others.

picks.why: Spay family estate on the Bopparder Hamm, the long loop of the Rhine at Boppard; its Riesling Grosses Gewächs comes from the Mandelstein, with the Feuerlay beside it.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Falstaff lists both the Mandelstein and the Feuerlay GG: confirm in two sources which leads and the label's form. The estate carries a living grower's name: say the family.

picks.why: Spay family estate making mostly dry and off dry Riesling from the Bopparder Hamm; the Feuerlay, a slate slope of the Hamm, is the site it is known by, in dry and sweet Prädikat styles.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Falstaff lists Bopparder Hamm Feuerlay Riesling Auslese: name the Prädikat the record teaches after the plan's words, from two sources, and say the family with no names.

picks.why: Oberwesel family estate of the slate gorge whose dry and off dry Rieslings come from the Engehöll and the Oelsberg; the Engehöll is the site it is known by.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS and not searched in this run: the region record names the Engehöll and the Oelsberg; confirm in two sources that the house still makes the Engehöll Riesling, whether as a Grosses Gewächs, and the label's form, else propose a swap with the checker.

picks.why: Stammersdorf estate with vines on the Bisamberg and the Nussberg, farmed biodynamically, that argued for the city's field blend as a fine wine; its Gemischter Satz from the Nussberg is that blend from one Ried.
picks.note: Confirm in two sources the house's part in the DAC of the 2013 vintage and the label's form for the years taught. Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Heiligenstadt Heuriger house, recorded as a farm in 1683 by its own account, where Ludwig van Beethoven (1770 to 1827) lodged in 1817; Weisser Marmor is its Riesling from the Nussberg, the city's Riesling bottled alone.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. The house's own page gives 1683: confirm the Beethoven stay of 1817 in two sources and the label's form (Weisser or Weißer Marmor); its Gemischter Satz from Ried Langteufel and Ried Preussen on the Nussberg goes in others. Tell the sale of 2006 as history with no living name.

picks.why: Grinzing estate on the slopes below the Cobenzl, tied to the City of Vienna; its Gemischter Satz from the Ried Reisenberg is the city's field blend from one of its named sites.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Falstaff lists the wine under Weingut Wien Cobenzl: confirm how the house writes its name, and tell the city's tie to the estate as history with its year from two sources, never as a present owner.

picks.why: Jedlersdorf family estate on the Bisamberg, on the Danube's left bank, with a large Heuriger; its Gemischter Satz from the Wiesthalen, an Erste Lage of the Österreichische Traditionsweingüter, is the left bank's field blend from one site.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Falstaff lists the Ried Wiesthalen year after year with the ÖTW's Erste Lage mark: write the level by its name only. Confirm the house's age and its Heuriger in two sources, and say the family with no names.

picks.why: Mauer family estate of the city's southern vineyards, farmed organically; its Gemischter Satz from the Kaasgraben is one of the field blends the city names by its site.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Falstaff lists the Kaasgraben under Bio Weingut Zahel: confirm in two sources where the Kaasgraben lies, that it leads the range, and the house's old mixed plantings on the Maurer Berg the region record names.

picks.why: Stetten family estate on the northern side of the Bisamberg in the southern Weinviertel, with Grüner Veltliner from Klassik to Reserve and reds beside it; the Hund is its Weinviertel DAC Reserve from one Ried.
picks.note: In doubt over the flagship: Decanter lists Ried Hund as a Weinviertel DAC Reserve, and the range also holds Goldjoch, Zeisen and Hommage. Confirm in two sources which Grüner Veltliner the house leads with, and the label's form; say the family with no names.

picks.why: Poysdorf family estate of the north, in the Weinviertel's Sekt town, making single Ried Grüner Veltliner and traditional method Sekt; the Bürsting is its Grüner Veltliner from one site.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Falstaff lists Grüner Veltliner Ried Bürsting: confirm in two sources that it leads and whether it carries the Weinviertel DAC; the Sekt goes in others. The couple who run it are living: say the family.

picks.why: Schrattenthal family estate near Retz in the far west of the Weinviertel; the Äussere Bergen is its Weinviertel DAC Reserve Grüner Veltliner from one Ried.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Falstaff lists the Weinviertel DAC Reserve Äussere Bergen in several years: confirm the site's soil before naming it (the region record says granite and loess for the house) and the label's form.

picks.why: Hohenwarth family estate on loess and limestone, known for old vine Grüner Veltliner; 8000 is its Weinviertel DAC Reserve from the Ried Laa.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Falstaff lists Grüner Veltliner Weinviertel DAC Reserve Ried Laa 8000 in several years: confirm in two sources what 8000 means (a planting density is the likely reading) and the label's word order.

picks.why: Röschitz family estate of the Retzer Land; its Weinviertel DAC Grüner Veltliner is the appellation's Klassik, the dry, peppery wine with the Pfefferl the DAC was made for, beside four Reserve and single Ried picks.
picks.note: Not searched in this run: confirm in two sources the house's Weinviertel DAC Klassik as its widely poured wine and the label's form (a village or Ried name may follow). If it cannot be confirmed, propose a swap with the checker (Weinrieder, for the cold north's Eiswein).

picks.why: Berghausen family estate of the Südsteiermark on the Slovenian border, with vines across it; its Sauvignon Blanc from the Zieregg, a steep Ried above the estate, carried the Südsteiermark onto lists abroad.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS and not searched in this run: confirm the Zieregg's soil before naming it, the label's form and its STK level, and the house's holdings in Slovenia, in two sources. Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Gamlitz family estate of the Südsteiermark; the Kranachberg gives its Sauvignon Blanc from one Ried, with the Sernauberg and its Morillon beside it.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS and not searched in this run: confirm the label's form and its STK level in two sources. Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Ratsch family estate of the Südsteiermark; its Sauvignon Blanc from the Nussberg, a steep Ried of the border hills, is the house's wine from one site.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS and not searched in this run: confirm the label's form, the soil and the STK level in two sources. This Nussberg is Styria's, not Vienna's of the Wien group: say so in a trap.

picks.why: Straden family estate of the Vulkanland Steiermark in the east; the Moarfeitl gives its Sauvignon Blanc from one Ried, beside its Saziani Grauburgunder.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Falstaff lists Sauvignon Blanc Vulkanland Steiermark DAC Ried Moarfeitl and Grauburgunder Ried Saziani, both as the STK's Grosse Lage: confirm the Moarfeitl's soil before naming it (the Vulkanland is not all volcanic) and the label's form.

picks.why: St. Stefan ob Stainz family estate of the Weststeiermark, known as Lex; its Schilcher, the piercing rosé of Blauer Wildbacher, is the Weststeiermark's own wine, made still and sparkling.
picks.note: In doubt over the wine's name: the house is known for Schilcher, but this run found no single Ried bottling by name. Confirm in two sources the Schilcher the house leads with (a Weststeiermark DAC Schilcher or a Riedenwein) and its exact label, else propose a swap with the checker. Name no living member of the family.
